sla_notes_intro: Pan-Africanism is a political and cultural movement that seeks unity, solidarity and liberation of Africans and people of African descent. Its meaning, objectives and importance explain many African struggles.
sla_notes_details: Pan-Africanism is the belief that Africans everywhere share a common history, fate and interests and should unite. Its objectives were to end slavery, racism and colonialism, to promote African unity and cooperation, to restore black dignity and culture and to achieve political and economic development. It is important because it inspired nationalism, produced organisations such as the OAU and the African Union, encouraged cultural pride (negritude) and supports cooperation in trade and security today. Debate on its relevance continues, focusing on integration and the African Continental Free Trade Area.
sla_notes_illustrations: A meeting of a school council where members from many classes unite to solve a problem shows how a common purpose creates strength, just as Pan-Africanists united to oppose colonial domination.
sla_notes_daily_life: The flags, songs and cooperation of African states in sport, trade and peacekeeping reflect Pan-Africanist ideas in everyday life.
sla_exercise: Define Pan-Africanism.::A movement that promotes unity, solidarity and liberation of Africans and people of African descent.||State two objectives of Pan-Africanism.::To end colonialism and racism and to promote African unity.||Name one organisation that came from Pan-Africanist ideas.::The Organisation of African Unity (now the African Union).

sla_notes_intro: Pan-Africanism originated from the suffering of Africans in the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade. Africans and their descendants in the New World began to share ideas of resistance and unity.
sla_notes_details: From the 15th century Europeans, beginning with the Portuguese, took millions of Africans to work on plantations and in mines in the Americas and the Caribbean. Enslaved people faced inhuman treatment, loss of identity, family separation and racial discrimination. Resistance took forms such as revolts (Haiti 1791), escapes and maroon communities, while shared suffering created a sense of common identity and solidarity among people of African origin. Their descendants in the New World later formed the first movements calling for freedom and a return to Africa.
sla_notes_illustrations: Olaudah Equiano, an enslaved African who bought his freedom, wrote about slavery and campaigned for abolition, an early example of black solidarity.
sla_notes_daily_life: Museums, memorials and heritage sites for slavery in places like Bagamoyo remind people of these origins.
sla_exercise: Which trade led to the origin of Pan-Africanism?::The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade.||Name one slave revolt in the New World.::The Haitian Revolution of 1791.||How did shared suffering influence Africans in the New World?::It created a common identity and solidarity.

sla_notes_intro: During the era of slavery and colonial systems in the New World, black people organised movements that promoted solidarity and freedom. These movements developed the ideas of Pan-Africanism.
sla_notes_details: Enslaved people and free blacks formed mutual aid societies and churches, such as the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and led revolts under leaders like Toussaint Louverture and Nat Turner. Abolitionist movements in Britain and America ended slavery in the 19th century (Britain 1833, USA 1865). The Back to Africa Movement led to settlements like Sierra Leone (1787) and Liberia (1847) and inspired thinkers such as Edward Blyden and Martin Delany. Black solidarity grew through writings, newspapers and conventions.
sla_notes_illustrations: Freed slaves resettled in Freetown, Sierra Leone, forming a black-ruled community that was seen as a symbol of black freedom.
sla_notes_daily_life: Names such as Freetown and Liberia's capital Monrovia still remind people of these events.
sla_exercise: Which country was founded as a settlement for freed slaves in 1847?::Liberia.||Name a leader of the Haitian revolution.::Toussaint Louverture.||What was the Back to Africa Movement?::A movement encouraging people of African descent to return and settle in Africa.

sla_notes_intro: In the early 20th century Pan-Africanism became an organised movement with conferences and leaders in the diaspora and Africa.
sla_notes_details: Henry Sylvester Williams organised the 1900 Pan-African Conference in London, W. E. B. Du Bois led Pan-African congresses (1919 to 1945), and Marcus Garvey's UNIA promoted black pride and the 'Africa for Africans' slogan. The Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester (1945) demanded independence with the participation of Kwame Nkrumah and Jomo Kenyatta. The movement moved from the diaspora to Africa, aiding nationalist parties, trade unions and newspapers, and it was helped by Italian invasion of Ethiopia (1935) and World War II experiences.
sla_notes_illustrations: At Manchester in 1945 delegates passed resolutions demanding self-government for colonies, and returned home to lead nationalist movements.
sla_notes_daily_life: This early organisation shows how education and communication help ordinary people to build movements for change.
sla_exercise: Who organised the first Pan-African Conference of 1900?::Henry Sylvester Williams.||Which congress in 1945 demanded African independence?::The Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester.||Name the organisation founded by Marcus Garvey.::The Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA).

sla_notes_intro: Pan-Africanism supported the fight against colonialism through conferences, resolutions and political solidarity. It linked African nationalists with the diaspora.
sla_notes_details: Pan-African congresses passed resolutions condemning colonial exploitation, racial discrimination and forced labour and demanded self-government. The 1945 Manchester resolutions inspired leaders of Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria and Malawi to form mass parties. Later conferences such as the All-African Peoples' Conference (Accra, 1958) supported independence movements and freedom fighters, and Ghana's independence (1957) gave hope to others. Pan-African ideas also produced the Pan-African Freedom Movement for East and Central Africa (PAFMECA) which supported Tanganyika, Uganda and Kenya.
sla_notes_illustrations: After the 1958 Accra conference, delegates carried the message of positive action back to their countries and set up committees to demand independence.
sla_notes_daily_life: Today's regional commemorations of independence anniversaries recall how solidarity brought freedom.
sla_exercise: Which conference in 1958 supported independence movements?::The All-African Peoples' Conference in Accra.||Which country was the first in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence, in 1957?::Ghana.||Name a regional organisation formed to support freedom in East and Central Africa.::PAFMECA.

sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: After independence Pan-Africanism focused on African unity, freeing the remaining colonies and fighting neo-colonialism and apartheid, then on economic integration in the era of globalisation.
sla_notes_details: The OAU was formed in 1963 to promote unity, defend sovereignty and end colonialism and apartheid; its Liberation Committee, based in Dar es Salaam, supported liberation movements in Mozambique, Angola, Zimbabwe, Namibia and South Africa. Neo-colonialism, meaning continued economic and political control by former rulers, was opposed by leaders such as Nkrumah and Nyerere (Arusha Declaration 1967). The OAU became the African Union in 2002 and regional communities such as SADC, EAC and ECOWAS were built. Africans face globalisation challenges such as unequal trade and debt and have adopted NEPAD and the AfCFTA.
sla_notes_illustrations: Tanzania hosted the OAU Liberation Committee and gave training camps and refuge to freedom fighters, for example ANC and FRELIMO.
sla_notes_daily_life: Cross-border trade, the EAC passport and shared institutions show Pan-Africanism in practice.
sla_exercise: When was the OAU formed?::1963.||What is neo-colonialism?::The continued economic or political control of independent countries by former colonial or foreign powers.||Where was the OAU Liberation Committee based?::Dar es Salaam.

sla_notes_intro: The Industrial Revolution was the change from hand production to machine-based factory production, which began in Britain in the 18th century. It transformed economies and societies.
sla_notes_details: It refers to the shift from agrarian and handicraft economies to industrial ones with mechanisation, use of new energy sources (coal and steam) and factory organisation. Processes included agricultural revolution, technological inventions (spinning jenny, water frame, steam engine, power loom), development of iron and steel, transport (canals, railways, steamships) and financial capital. Characteristics were factory production, urbanisation, division of labour, growth of the working class and capitalists, mass production, expanded trade and new inventions.
sla_notes_illustrations: In Lancashire, cotton was spun and woven by machines in factories, so cloth was produced faster and more cheaply than in cottages.
sla_notes_daily_life: The clothes, bicycles and trains in daily life are descendants of the innovations of the Industrial Revolution.
sla_exercise: Where did the Industrial Revolution begin?::Britain.||Name two inventions of the industrial revolution.::The steam engine and the spinning jenny.||State one characteristic of the industrial revolution.::Factory production or urbanisation.

sla_name: Britain's Revolution Compared with Other Countries
sla_assessment_criteria: The industrial revolutions of Britain and Belgium, France, Germany, USA and Japan are well compared.
sla_teaching_aids: Written documents|Written texts in braille on industries
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Industrialisation did not happen the same way everywhere. Britain led, and Belgium, France, Germany, the USA and Japan followed with their own patterns.
sla_notes_details: Britain had coal and iron, colonies for raw materials and markets, capital, political stability, a navy, and inventions. Belgium industrialised early because of coal, iron and rail, France industrialised more slowly due to the revolution, small farms and wars, and Germany industrialised rapidly after unification in 1871 with state support, banks and technical education, especially in steel, chemicals and electricity. The USA grew after the Civil War with large resources, immigrant labour, railways and mass production, and Japan industrialised after the Meiji Restoration (1868) through state-led modernisation, learning from the West and building factories, shipping and armaments. Differences lay in speed, state role, energy, capital and market.
sla_notes_illustrations: Comparison chart: Britain (private enterprise, colonies), Germany (banks and state, science), Japan (state factories sold to zaibatsu), showing differing paths.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding different models helps students to discuss how developing countries can plan their own industrial policies.
sla_exercise: Name two factors that favoured industrialisation in Britain.::Coal and iron resources and colonies for raw materials and markets.||What event started rapid industrialisation in Japan?::The Meiji Restoration of 1868.||Which country united in 1871 and then industrialised rapidly?::Germany.

sla_notes_intro: The industrial revolutions changed the world economically, socially and politically. Some changes were positive and others harmful.
sla_notes_details: Economically they raised production and trade, created capitalism, banks, insurance and transport networks and led to the search for raw materials and markets. Socially they caused urbanisation, slums, child labour, new classes, trade unions and improvements in health and education later. Politically they increased colonial expansion and the Scramble for Africa, rivalry among powers and reforms such as factory acts and the extension of voting rights. In Africa they led to the destruction of local industries, the introduction of cash crops and exploitation of resources. Environmental damage such as pollution also began.
sla_notes_illustrations: The demand for cotton in Lancashire led to cotton growing being imposed in colonies like Tanganyika.
sla_notes_daily_life: Modern cities, railways, and global trade all trace part of their origin to these revolutions.
sla_exercise: State one social effect of the Industrial Revolution.::Urbanisation and growth of slums (or child labour, trade unions).||How did the Industrial Revolution affect Africa?::It led to colonisation and exploitation of resources and markets.||Name one political effect.::Colonial expansion or reforms such as Factory Acts.

sla_notes_intro: Industrial revolutions continued in the 20th century with new technologies, especially in Asia and Latin America. They changed the world economy.
sla_notes_details: The Second Industrial Revolution (electricity, steel, chemicals, oil, assembly line) was followed by a third based on electronics, computers and automation. Asian countries such as Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore (Asian Tigers), China and India industrialised through state planning, export-oriented policies, education and investment in technology. Latin America (Brazil, Argentina, Mexico) used import substitution industrialisation and later opened to foreign capital. Impacts included growth of multinational corporations, expansion of world trade, migration to cities, increased incomes and inequalities, and environmental pressures.
sla_notes_illustrations: South Korea moved from a poor agricultural economy in the 1950s to a major exporter of ships, cars and electronics by the 1990s through planned industrial policy.
sla_notes_daily_life: Most electronics used daily, like phones and televisions, are products of these revolutions and often manufactured in Asia.
sla_exercise: Name two Asian Tigers.::South Korea and Taiwan (or Singapore, Hong Kong).||What was import substitution?::Producing locally goods that were previously imported.||Give one impact of 20th century industrialisation.::Growth of world trade or environmental pollution.

sla_notes_intro: Comparing the industrial revolutions shows what changed and what remained the same. It helps to understand the direction of world economic development.
sla_notes_details: Changes include energy (coal and steam to electricity, oil, nuclear), technologies (mechanical to electronic and automated), and leading nations (Britain to USA, Germany, Japan and later Asia). The state became more involved, and corporations and finance grew. Continuities include the search for profit, capitalist relations, exploitation of raw materials, unequal exchange between industrial and non-industrial regions, urbanisation and environmental damage. Both eras improved productivity but produced inequality.
sla_notes_illustrations: A table with two columns titled changes and continuities lists the steam engine versus the electric motor, and the constant search for cheap labour and markets.
sla_notes_daily_life: Workers today still face issues similar to workers in early factories, such as safety and fair wages.
sla_exercise: Give one change between the two eras.::Energy shifted from coal and steam to electricity and oil.||Give one continuity.::Capitalist profit motives or exploitation of raw materials.||Which countries became new industrial leaders in the 20th century?::The USA, Germany, Japan and later Asian economies.

sla_notes_intro: The Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) is the current wave of change that merges digital, physical and biological technologies. It is evolving in the 21st century.
sla_notes_details: Its nature is the fusion of technologies such as artificial intelligence, robotics, the Internet of Things, big data, 3D printing, blockchain, biotechnology and renewable energy. Characteristics are speed (exponential change), breadth of impact across sectors, systems-level transformation, automation and connectivity. Unlike earlier revolutions, it depends on data and knowledge and creates new industries as well as threatens jobs.
sla_notes_illustrations: A smart farm uses sensors, drones and mobile apps to monitor soil and crops, showing the merging of digital and physical technologies.
sla_notes_daily_life: Smartphones, mobile money and online learning are everyday examples of the Fourth Industrial Revolution.
sla_exercise: What technologies characterise the 4IR?::Artificial intelligence, robotics, and the Internet of Things.||How is 4IR different from earlier revolutions?::It fuses digital, physical and biological technologies and moves faster.||Give one example of a 4IR technology in daily life.::Mobile money or smartphones.

sla_notes_intro: The Fourth Industrial Revolution is changing socio-economic and political patterns worldwide through digital technology.
sla_notes_details: Impacts include the smart economy (automation, platform businesses, digital trade), e-government (online services, taxes, identity), e-commerce, fintech and mobile money, and new employment types along with job losses in routine work. It raises questions on privacy, cybersecurity, digital divide, inequality, and skills. Politically, it changes participation through social media and challenges regulation. Countries respond with digital strategies, ICT in education and innovation hubs.
sla_notes_illustrations: A citizen renews a business licence online through an e-government portal instead of queuing at an office, saving time and cost.
sla_notes_daily_life: Online shopping and cashless payments show these changes in daily life.

sla_notes_intro: Since independence, African countries have tried to industrialise, with mixed success. The nature and character of this development reflect colonial inheritance and policy choices.
sla_notes_details: Colonial economies focused on exporting raw materials, so African industries were few. After 1960 governments adopted import substitution, state-owned enterprises, and in Tanzania the Arusha Declaration with nationalisation. In the 1980s structural adjustment programmes led to liberalisation and privatisation. Recent strategies include industrial parks, special economic zones, value addition, regional integration and Vision 2025. Constraints include shortage of capital, technology, energy, infrastructure, skills, small markets, debt and dependence on foreign markets, while some countries such as Ethiopia, Egypt and South Africa made progress.
sla_notes_illustrations: Tanzania's textile factories of the 1970s, such as Urafiki, illustrate the state-led approach, and later privatisation illustrates the liberalisation phase.
sla_notes_daily_life: Locally produced goods such as cement, beverages and textiles reflect African industrial development.
sla_exercise: What did colonial economies in Africa emphasise?::Production of raw materials for export.||Name one constraint to industrial growth in Africa.::Shortage of capital, energy or skills.||What is a special economic zone?::An area with special incentives to attract investment and manufacturing.

sla_notes_intro: Africa can learn from earlier industrial revolutions to plan its own industrial development. Lessons come from Europe, Asia and other regions.
sla_notes_details: Lessons include the importance of agriculture as a base for industry, investment in education, science and technology, infrastructure such as energy and transport, a strong role of the state in planning and protection of infant industries, access to finance and markets, good governance and stability, environmental care and labour protection. Africa should build local value chains, avoid over-reliance on raw exports and promote regional integration. It should also adapt 4IR technologies to leapfrog stages.
sla_notes_illustrations: Following the Asian Tigers, a country invests in schools and technical training, builds ports and power, and targets exports of processed goods.
sla_notes_daily_life: The lessons apply to a village that decides to process fruit into juice rather than sell raw fruit.
sla_exercise: Name one lesson Africa can learn from Asia.::Invest in education and technology.||Why is value addition important?::It raises earnings by selling processed goods rather than raw materials.||What infrastructure supports industry?::Energy, roads, railways and ports.

sla_notes_intro: Administration is the organisation and management of the affairs of a group or state, and an administrative system is the structure through which authority is exercised.
sla_notes_details: Administration involves making and implementing decisions, keeping order, collecting resources and delivering services. An administrative system consists of institutions, rules, leaders and procedures, and may be centralised or decentralised, monarchical, republican, democratic or authoritarian. Elements include the leader or head, advisors, officials, army or police, courts, and taxation. Systems differ according to history, culture, geography and religion.
sla_notes_illustrations: A school has a headteacher, deputy, teachers and prefects, a small administrative system with clear roles and rules.
sla_notes_daily_life: Village leadership, local councils and the district commissioner's office are administrative systems people meet daily.
sla_exercise: Define administration.::The organisation and management of the affairs of a state or group.||Name two elements of an administrative system.::Leaders and institutions (also rules, courts, army).||Give one example of a local administrative unit.::A village council or a ward.

sla_notes_intro: Before modern states many societies had their own administrative systems. Studying them shows diverse ways of governing.
sla_notes_details: In pre-colonial Africa there were centralised kingdoms (Buganda, Asante, Zulu, Ethiopia), chiefdoms with councils of elders and stateless or segmentary societies governed by age-sets and clan elders. Ancient Europe had Greek city-states, the Roman Republic and Empire, and later feudal monarchies. South America had the Inca and Aztec empires with taxation and road networks, Asia had dynastic China with a civil service and India's Mauryan empire, and the Middle East had caliphates and Persian satraps. These systems used tribute, military service, courts and religion for legitimacy.
sla_notes_illustrations: The Buganda kingdom had a Kabaka assisted by a Katikiro and chiefs administering counties, showing a centralised African system.
sla_notes_daily_life: Traditional councils and elders' courts still resolve disputes in many communities.

sla_notes_intro: Religion and administration are closely related because religion provides beliefs and values that justify authority and guide law.
sla_notes_details: Religion gave rulers legitimacy through ideas like divine right or being God's representative, provided moral codes and laws, and created institutions such as priesthoods, mosques and churches that took part in governance, education and taxation. Rulers used religion to unify people, and religious leaders sometimes advised or challenged rulers. In theocracies religion and government are one, while in others they are separate.
sla_notes_illustrations: The Egyptian pharaoh was seen as a god-king, whose commands were considered divine, showing the link between religion and rule.
sla_notes_daily_life: Prayers at national events and religious leaders' roles in peace-building show the link today.

sla_notes_intro: From the Middle Ages to the 18th century religions shaped administrative systems in many regions. They introduced new laws, institutions and ideas.
sla_notes_details: Christianity in medieval Europe led to church-state relations with the Pope and kings, canon law and church lands. Islam produced caliphates and sultanates based on Sharia, the shura and zakat, spreading along the East African coast. Buddhism influenced Asian kingdoms such as Ashoka's India, Confucianism shaped China's civil service with moral governance, Shintoism supported the Japanese emperor's divinity, Judaism guided ancient Hebrew law, and indigenous African religions supported kingship through rituals. The extent of influence varied: religion was decisive in some societies and limited in others.
sla_notes_illustrations: The sultanate of Zanzibar and Kilwa used Islamic law and Muslim scholars in administration and trade.
sla_notes_daily_life: Laws on marriage and inheritance in many countries still reflect religious principles.
sla_exercise: Which religion influenced the Sultanate of Kilwa?::Islam.||How did Confucianism influence China?::It promoted moral leadership and an exam-based civil service.||Name one Buddhist ruler who applied religious principles.::Ashoka of India.

sla_notes_intro: Between the 15th and 19th centuries many societies moved from governance based on religion to secular systems based on reason and law.
sla_notes_details: Causes included the Renaissance, the Reformation (which broke the Pope's power), the Enlightenment (ideas of Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau), scientific advances, the rise of nation states and capitalism and revolutions. Secular systems separate church and state, base authority on constitutions, elected representatives and human rights, and use a professional bureaucracy. The transition was gradual and sometimes violent, as in the English and French revolutions, and led to reforms in law, education and taxation.
sla_notes_illustrations: The French Revolution's Declaration of the Rights of Man (1789) replaced divine right with popular sovereignty.
sla_notes_daily_life: Modern constitutions guarantee freedom of worship while government remains neutral in religion.
sla_exercise: Name one Enlightenment thinker.::John Locke (or Montesquieu, Rousseau).||What does secular mean?::Not based on or controlled by religion.||Which movement broke the power of the Pope in Europe?::The Reformation.

sla_notes_intro: Slavery and feudalism were systems in which labour and land were controlled by ruling classes. They shaped social and political life.
sla_notes_details: In slavery, slaves were owned as property and forced to work without pay (ancient Greece, Rome, plantation slavery). In feudalism, kings gave land (fiefs) to lords in return for military service and loyalty, and peasants (serfs) worked the land and were tied to it. The feudal hierarchy was king, nobles, knights and serfs, with manorial economy and church influence. Both relied on agriculture and unfree labour, and political power was linked to ownership of land and people.
sla_notes_illustrations: A medieval manor had a lord, a village of serfs who farmed the lord's fields three days a week and paid dues, illustrating feudal obligations.
sla_notes_daily_life: The idea of landlord and tenant today has a distant link with feudal land relations.
sla_exercise: What is a fief?::Land granted by a king or lord in return for loyalty and military service.||Who were serfs?::Peasants tied to the land of a lord who worked for him.||Give one difference between a slave and a serf.::A slave is owned as property, while a serf is bound to land but not sold individually.

sla_notes_intro: Slavery and feudalism produced new forms of administration in Western Europe, Asia and Africa up to the 19th century.
sla_notes_details: In Western Europe feudal monarchies developed into centralised absolute states as kings built armies, taxation and bureaucracies; parliaments arose from feudal councils (English Magna Carta 1215). Slave-based plantation economies produced colonial governments, laws such as slave codes and administrative controls. In Asia, Japanese feudalism under shoguns and daimyo, and Indian and Chinese landlord systems shaped rule. In Africa, slavery and slave trade produced strong states (Dahomey, Asante, Zanzibar sultanate) and warlord systems but also weakened others through wars and depopulation.
sla_notes_illustrations: Magna Carta limited the power of King John, showing how feudal relations between king and barons produced constitutional ideas.
sla_notes_daily_life: Ideas about limiting rulers' power inform our modern democratic systems.
sla_exercise: What document limited the king's power in England in 1215?::The Magna Carta.||Name a state in West Africa that grew through slave trading.::Dahomey (or Asante).||Who were the shoguns?::Military rulers of feudal Japan.

sla_notes_intro: The English and French revolutions ended absolute monarchy in favour of limited or republican government. They influenced the world.
sla_notes_details: The English revolution (Civil War 1642-49, Glorious Revolution 1688) established parliamentary supremacy and the Bill of Rights (1689), and the French Revolution (1789) ended feudal privileges, introduced the Declaration of the Rights of Man, republic and the nation state. Lessons include the importance of constitutions, rule of law, separation of powers, citizens' rights and popular participation. They also showed dangers of violence and instability. Ideas spread to colonies and shaped nationalism.
sla_notes_illustrations: The French motto liberty, equality and fraternity inspired later independence movements, including in Haiti.
sla_notes_daily_life: Modern election of leaders and courts protecting rights derive partly from these revolutions.
sla_exercise: Which English event of 1688 limited royal power?::The Glorious Revolution.||Name one lesson from the French Revolution.::The importance of citizens' rights and equality before the law.||What was the French motto?::Liberty, equality and fraternity.

sla_notes_intro: The rise of capitalism, an economic system based on private ownership and profit, changed politics and administration.
sla_notes_details: Capitalism grew from commercial revolution, trade, enclosure of land, mercantilism, banking and industrial growth. The bourgeoisie, a wealthy middle class, demanded political power and supported revolutions that ended feudal restrictions. New administrations promoted free markets, property rights, standardised laws, patents, taxation and colonial expansion. Socio-economic changes included wage labour, urbanisation and class conflict, and states created ministries of trade and finance.
sla_notes_illustrations: British merchants and factory owners pushed for the Reform Act of 1832 to gain a share in parliament.
sla_notes_daily_life: The laws that protect property, contracts and businesses have roots in the rise of capitalism.
sla_exercise: Who were the bourgeoisie?::The wealthy middle class of merchants and industrialists.||Name one change capitalism brought to labour.::Wage labour.||What was mercantilism?::An economic policy that sought to increase national wealth through trade and colonies.

sla_notes_intro: Economic crises in capitalism in the 20th century produced new political systems, both reactionary and revolutionary.
sla_notes_details: Crises such as post-First World War inflation and the Great Depression (1929) caused unemployment, poverty and unrest. Reactionary responses included Fascism in Italy (Mussolini) and Nazism in Germany (Hitler), which used nationalism, dictatorship, racism and militarism to preserve the capitalist order. Revolutionary responses included Socialism and Communism, as in the Russian Revolution (1917), based on public ownership and planned economy. Capitalism also reformed through welfare states and the New Deal.
sla_notes_illustrations: Germany's unemployment reached six million by 1932, helping Hitler win support with promises of jobs and national revival.
sla_notes_daily_life: Modern social security systems trace back to responses to economic crises.
sla_exercise: In which year did the Great Depression begin?::1929.||Name two fascist leaders.::Mussolini and Hitler.||What is socialism?::A system in which the means of production are owned or controlled by the community or state.

sla_notes_intro: The 20th century systems inspired new ideologies, some of which led to discrimination, conflict and struggle.
sla_notes_details: Apartheid in South Africa (1948 to 1994) was a system of racial segregation and white domination influenced by racist doctrines, and it was opposed by the ANC, Pan-Africanists and international solidarity until its end. Zionism, a nationalist movement founded by Theodor Herzl (1897), aimed at a Jewish homeland, was strengthened by European anti-Semitism and Nazi persecution and led to the state of Israel in 1948 and to the Palestinian conflict. Their impact included population removal, violence, international debates and changes in international law and human rights.
sla_notes_illustrations: The Sharpeville massacre (1960) and the Soweto uprising (1976) show resistance to apartheid.
sla_notes_daily_life: Anti-discrimination laws and campaigns for equality continue to draw on the lessons of these ideologies.

sla_notes_intro: After independence African states adopted various administrative systems which changed over time.
sla_notes_details: Most inherited colonial structures with centralised bureaucracies. Many adopted one-party systems in the 1960s and 1970s for national unity (Tanzania's TANU/CCM), military regimes appeared in some countries, and socialist experiments such as Ujamaa were tried. In the 1990s pressures for multiparty democracy, economic liberalisation and good governance led to constitutional reforms, decentralisation, elections and civil society growth. Challenges include corruption, weak institutions, ethnic divisions and coups, but there are also progress in regional cooperation and accountability.
sla_notes_illustrations: Tanzania moved from a one-party system to multiparty politics in 1992 with a constitutional change.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local government elections and district councils are examples of decentralised administration.

sla_notes_intro: Threats to world peace are actions, conditions or events that endanger the peaceful coexistence of nations and the security of people. Understanding their meaning and features is the basis for studying wars and conflicts.
sla_notes_details: Peace means the absence of war and the presence of justice, security and cooperation, while security is protection from danger and fear. Threats include wars, arms races, terrorism, ethnic and civil conflicts, economic and resource competition, ideological rivalry, cyber attacks and pandemics. Features are violence or the threat of violence, involvement of states or non-state actors, cross-border effects, destruction of life and property, refugee flows and disruption of the economy. Threats may be traditional, mainly military and between states, or non-traditional.
sla_notes_illustrations: A border dispute between two countries that leads to troop build-up, closed trade routes and thousands of refugees is a threat to peace showing the features of violence, cross-border effects and displacement.
sla_notes_daily_life: Even quarrels in the community that escalate into violence show how threats to peace begin with unresolved conflicts.
sla_exercise: Define peace.::Absence of war together with justice, security and cooperation.||Give two examples of threats to world peace.::War and terrorism.||State one feature of threats to peace.::Violence with destruction of life and property (or displacement of people).

sla_notes_intro: Between the 17th and 19th centuries Europe experienced major wars that changed borders and the balance of power. The Thirty Years War, the Napoleonic wars and the Franco-Prussian war are examples.
sla_notes_details: The Thirty Years War (1618-1648) started as a religious conflict between Catholics and Protestants in the Holy Roman Empire and became a struggle for power involving Sweden, France and Spain, with huge destruction. The Napoleonic wars (1799-1815) arose from French revolutionary expansion, ended at Waterloo, and reorganised Europe. The Franco-Prussian war (1870-71) resulted from rivalry between France and Prussia and led to German unification and French humiliation. Impacts included loss of life, changes in boundaries, new balance of power, nationalism and future rivalries and the creation of new states.
sla_notes_illustrations: After the defeat at Sedan in 1871, France lost Alsace-Lorraine and the German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles, planting the seeds of the First World War.
sla_notes_daily_life: Remembrance of these wars in European museums shows how wars change generations.

sla_notes_intro: The great wars of the 17th to 19th centuries gave rise to ideas and agreements to reduce conflict. They laid a foundation for international relations.
sla_notes_details: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) ended the Thirty Years War and established the principle of state sovereignty and non-interference in internal affairs. After Napoleon, the Congress of Vienna (1815) applied the balance of power, in which no single state dominates, and led to the Concert of Europe and military alliances such as the Holy Alliance. These ideas influenced later diplomacy, treaties and international law but alliances also increased rivalry.
sla_notes_illustrations: At Vienna, the great powers restored monarchies, redrew borders to balance France, and agreed to meet regularly to solve disputes.
sla_notes_daily_life: The idea of respecting borders and negotiating conflicts is the basis of the United Nations Charter.
sla_exercise: What did the Treaty of Westphalia establish?::The principle of state sovereignty.||What is the balance of power?::A system in which power is distributed so that no state dominates others.||Which congress reorganised Europe after Napoleon?::The Congress of Vienna (1815).

sla_notes_intro: From the late 19th century colonial rivalry and alliances led to two world wars. These conflicts undermined world peace.
sla_notes_details: Causes of the First World War (1914-18) included colonial rivalries, militarism, alliances (Triple Entente and Triple Alliance), nationalism and the assassination at Sarajevo. The Manchuria crisis (1931), when Japan invaded China, showed the weakness of the League of Nations, and dictators in Italy, Germany and Japan pursued aggression (Ethiopia 1935, Rhineland 1936). The Second World War (1939-45) began with the invasion of Poland and the policy of appeasement. Millions died, including in the Holocaust, and Africans and Asians were involved in fighting and forced labour. The wars ended empires and started decolonisation.
sla_notes_illustrations: Africans from Tanganyika served as carriers and soldiers in the First World War campaign against the Germans in East Africa.
sla_notes_daily_life: War memorials and cemeteries in Tanzanian towns remind communities of the world wars.

sla_notes_intro: Statesmen and nations made efforts to prevent wars between the late 19th century and the 1940s through conferences, treaties and organisations.
sla_notes_details: The Berlin Conference (1884-85) aimed to regulate colonial competition in Africa without war but caused partition. After the First World War, the Versailles Peace Treaty (1919) punished Germany and created new states, and the League of Nations (1920) aimed at collective security and disarmament but failed because of the absence of major powers, lack of an army and inability to stop aggression. After the Second World War the United Nations (1945) was created with the Security Council, General Assembly and specialised agencies to maintain peace, promote human rights and development. The Charter bans use of force except in self-defence.
sla_notes_illustrations: The UN Security Council sends peacekeepers to conflict zones, which the League could not do.
sla_notes_daily_life: Tanzanian peacekeepers serve in UN missions in Africa today.
sla_exercise: Which organisation preceded the United Nations?::The League of Nations.||Name one weakness of the League of Nations.::It had no army or major powers such as the USA were absent.||In which year was the UN formed?::1945.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the history of threats to world peace
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the history of conflicts and wars of the 20th Century
learning_activity_name: Examine the extent to which cold war politics and the arms race threatened world peace and security from the 1940s to the 1990s
sla_name: Cold War Politics and the Arms Race
sla_assessment_criteria: The cold war politics and the arms race that threatened world peace and security from the 1940s to the 1990s are clearly examined.
sla_teaching_aids: Online resources on cold war politics|The arms race threatened world peace|Security from the 1940s to the 1990s
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The Cold War (1945-1991) was a rivalry between the USA-led West and the Soviet-led East that threatened world peace without direct war between the superpowers.
sla_notes_details: It was caused by ideological differences (capitalism versus communism), mistrust after the Second World War, the division of Germany, the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan, and the formation of NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955). Its features were the arms race including nuclear weapons, proxy wars (Korea, Vietnam, Angola, Afghanistan), crises such as the Berlin Blockade and Cuban Missile Crisis (1962), space race and spying. The threat of nuclear war and the diversion of resources hindered development in many countries.
sla_notes_illustrations: In the Cuban Missile Crisis, the USA and USSR came close to nuclear war over Soviet missiles in Cuba until an agreement was reached.
sla_notes_daily_life: Cold War rivalry influenced conflicts in Africa, for example in Angola and Mozambique, affecting the countries near Tanzania.
sla_exercise: Name the two Cold War military alliances.::NATO and the Warsaw Pact.||What was the Cuban Missile Crisis?::A 1962 confrontation between the USA and the USSR over Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba.||What is a proxy war?::A war in which major powers support opposing sides in another country.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the history of threats to world peace
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the history of conflicts and wars of the 20th Century
learning_activity_name: Examine the efforts made to overcome threats to world peace caused by cold war politics and the arms race (Nuclear Proliferation Treaties SALT I, SALT II, Camp David Peace Accord 1979 and Oslo Accord 1993)
sla_name: Efforts to Overcome Cold War Threats and the Arms Race
sla_assessment_criteria: The efforts to overcome threats to world peace and security caused by cold war politics and the arms race are well examined.
sla_teaching_aids: ICT devices with contents on the improvement of relationship between the antagonists of the cold war
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Nations pursued treaties and diplomacy to reduce the nuclear danger and settle conflicts during and after the Cold War.
sla_notes_details: Nuclear proliferation treaties include the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963), the Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968), and the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks (SALT I in 1972 and SALT II in 1979) between the USA and USSR. Détente, hotlines and summit meetings reduced tension, and the Cold War ended with disarmament treaties such as INF (1987) and the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the collapse of the USSR (1991). Peace agreements such as the Camp David Accord (1979) between Egypt and Israel and the Oslo Accord (1993) between Israel and the PLO aimed to settle Middle East conflicts, though they left issues unresolved.
sla_notes_illustrations: In 1979 President Sadat of Egypt and Prime Minister Begin of Israel signed the Camp David agreement mediated by US President Carter.
sla_notes_daily_life: The reduction of nuclear stockpiles and peace talks show how negotiations can prevent disasters.
sla_exercise: What did SALT stand for?::Strategic Arms Limitation Talks.||Which accord in 1979 was between Egypt and Israel?::The Camp David Peace Accord.||In which year did the USSR collapse?::1991.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the history of threats to world peace
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of new threats to world peace and security
learning_activity_name: Examine the rise of new threats to world peace and security (terrorism and asymmetric war, cyber security, radicalism)
sla_name: New Threats to World Peace and Security
sla_assessment_criteria: The rise of new threats to world peace and security is clearly examined.
sla_teaching_aids: ICT devices with contents on terrorism|Cyber security
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: After the Cold War new threats emerged that are not simply wars between states. They include terrorism, cyber insecurity and radicalism.
sla_notes_details: Terrorism is the use of violence against civilians for political aims, carried out by groups such as Al-Qaeda, Boko Haram and Al-Shabaab, and the attacks of 11 September 2001 changed global security policy. Asymmetric war is fighting between unequal opponents using guerrilla tactics. Cyber security threats include hacking, ransomware and attacks on infrastructure and elections. Radicalism is extreme ideology leading to violence, spread through the internet and poverty. Other threats are piracy, human trafficking, drug trafficking and pandemics.
sla_notes_illustrations: The 1998 bombings of the US embassies in Dar es Salaam and Nairobi are examples of terrorism affecting East Africa.
sla_notes_daily_life: Personal internet safety and community vigilance help to fight the new threats.
sla_exercise: Define terrorism.::The use of violence against civilians to achieve political goals.||What is asymmetric war?::War between opponents of very unequal strength, often using guerrilla methods.||Give one example of a cyber security threat.::Hacking or ransomware attacks.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the history of threats to world peace
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of new threats to world peace and security
learning_activity_name: Discuss the differences between traditional and new threats to world peace and security (nature, character and pattern)
sla_name: Traditional versus New Threats to Peace
sla_assessment_criteria: Differences between traditional and new threats to world peace and security in terms of nature, character and pattern are clearly discussed.
sla_teaching_aids: Written texts on traditional|New threat to world peace
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Traditional and new threats differ in their nature, character and pattern. Comparing them helps in choosing suitable responses.
sla_notes_details: Traditional threats involve states, standing armies, conventional weapons, defined battlefields and declared wars, and are tackled by diplomacy and military alliances. New threats involve non-state actors, networks, unconventional methods (suicide attacks, cyber attacks), unpredictable targets including civilians, transnational reach and use of technology and social media. Their pattern is diffuse rather than a clear front line. Traditional threats need state-to-state agreements, while new threats require intelligence, cooperation, law enforcement and tackling root causes.
sla_notes_illustrations: A table comparing the Franco-Prussian war (states, armies, open battles) with a cyber attack on a bank (hidden actors, no borders).
sla_notes_daily_life: A community may face a conventional dispute with a neighbour or a modern threat like online fraud, each requiring different responses.
sla_exercise: Give one feature of traditional threats.::They involve states and armies.||Give one feature of new threats.::They involve non-state actors and unconventional methods.||Why are new threats harder to solve?::They are diffuse, transnational and unpredictable.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the history of threats to world peace
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of new threats to world peace and security
learning_activity_name: Discuss strategies to overcome new threats to world peace and security
sla_name: Strategies to Overcome New Threats to Peace
sla_assessment_criteria: strategies to overcome new threats to world peace and security are clearly discussed.
sla_teaching_aids: Written texts on strategies to overcome new threats
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: New threats require cooperation among states, institutions and communities. Various strategies are used to prevent and respond to them.
sla_notes_details: Strategies include international counter-terrorism conventions and UN Security Council resolutions, intelligence sharing, border control and financial monitoring, cyber security laws and digital forensics, regional forces such as the African Union Mission in Somalia, and peacekeeping. Long-term measures address root causes through education, poverty reduction, job creation, good governance, human rights and de-radicalisation programmes and community policing. Media literacy and international law enforcement help to counter online radicalism.
sla_notes_illustrations: Countries of the East African Community share intelligence and harmonise laws to fight terrorism.
sla_notes_daily_life: Reporting suspicious activity and teaching young people about tolerance are practical community strategies.
sla_exercise: Name one international response to terrorism.::UN counter-terrorism resolutions (or intelligence sharing).||How can poverty reduction help fight radicalism?::It removes conditions that push people into extremist groups.||Name one regional force that fights terrorism in Africa.::AMISOM (African Union Mission in Somalia).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the history of threats to world peace
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the threats to world peace resulting from civil and ethnic wars
learning_activity_name: Examine the nature and character of ethnic and civil wars and the threats they pose on world peace and security (Kosovo conflict, Rwanda and Burundi Civil Wars, Somalia, Central Africa Republic, Mali, Rohingya, Cambodia, Yemen, the Palestinian-Israel conflict)
sla_name: Ethnic and Civil Wars and Threats to World Peace
sla_assessment_criteria: The nature and character of ethnic and civil wars and threats to world peace and security is clearly examined.
sla_teaching_aids: ICT devices with contents on ethnic|Inter-ethnic wars
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Ethnic and civil wars occur within states but their effects spread across borders. Their nature and character make them threats to international peace.
sla_notes_details: Causes include ethnic discrimination, competition for power and resources, weak governance, colonial legacies and external interference. Cases include the Kosovo conflict (1998-99), the Rwanda genocide (1994) and Burundi civil war, Somalia, the Central African Republic, Mali, the Rohingya crisis in Myanmar, Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge, Yemen and the Israel-Palestine conflict. Features are massacres, genocide, refugee movements, regional instability, humanitarian crises, and arms trade.
sla_notes_illustrations: During the 1994 Rwanda genocide about 800,000 people were killed and more than a million fled to neighbouring countries including Tanzania, straining resources and security.
sla_notes_daily_life: Communities hosting refugees experience such effects directly, making peace a local concern too.
sla_exercise: In which year did the Rwanda genocide occur?::1994.||Name two effects of civil wars on neighbouring countries.::Refugee flows and regional instability.||Which country did the Khmer Rouge rule?::Cambodia.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the history of threats to world peace
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the threats to world peace resulting from civil and ethnic wars
learning_activity_name: Examine the extent to which ethnic and civil wars are connected to the global industrial-military complex
sla_name: Ethnic and Civil Wars and the Global Industrial-Military Complex
sla_assessment_criteria: The connection between ethnic and civil wars to global industrial military complex is well examined.
sla_teaching_aids: Online resources on the relationship between ethnic wars|Global industrial military complex
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Many modern conflicts are linked to global networks of arms production and trade. This is often called the industrial-military complex.
sla_notes_details: The term describes the close relationship among the armed forces, arms manufacturers and governments, in which industries profit from war and influence policy. Large arms producers (USA, Russia, France, China, UK) sell weapons to governments and rebels, often through illegal channels, prolonging wars in Africa, the Middle East and Asia. Resources such as diamonds, oil and coltan finance wars (conflict resources). Arms-control treaties and embargoes attempt to limit trade but enforcement is weak.
sla_notes_illustrations: Small arms sold in one conflict find their way to other conflict zones, as happened in the Great Lakes region.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local violence and banditry are often fuelled by illegal small arms circulating across borders.
sla_exercise: What is the industrial-military complex?::The relationship between the military, arms industries and government that benefits from war.||Name one resource that funds conflicts.::Diamonds (or oil or coltan).||Why is arms trade a threat to peace?::It supplies weapons that prolong and intensify conflicts.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the history of threats to world peace
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the threats to world peace resulting from civil and ethnic wars
learning_activity_name: Discuss peace building strategies in countries affected by ethnic and civil wars
sla_name: Peace-building in Countries Affected by Civil and Ethnic Wars
sla_assessment_criteria: The peace building strategies are well discussed.
sla_teaching_aids: Online resources on peace building strategies
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Peace-building consists of actions to end violence and rebuild trust and institutions after conflict. It aims to prevent conflict from returning.
sla_notes_details: Strategies include peace agreements and mediation (Arusha Peace Agreement for Burundi 2000), ceasefire monitoring and peacekeeping, disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of fighters, transitional justice including tribunals (ICTR in Arusha) and truth commissions (South Africa), power-sharing governments, reforms of security and judiciary, reconciliation programmes, reconstruction and economic recovery, and support for refugees' return. Regional bodies such as the AU and EAC and civil society play major roles.
sla_notes_illustrations: The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, based in Arusha, tried leaders responsible for genocide, promoting accountability.
sla_notes_daily_life: Community dialogue, sports and traditional courts such as Gacaca help neighbours to reconcile.
sla_exercise: What is DDR?::Disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of fighters.||Where was the ICTR based?::Arusha, Tanzania.||Why is reconciliation important?::It rebuilds trust between former enemies and prevents a return to violence.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the history of development in Africa
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the history of development in post-colonial Africa
learning_activity_name: Explain the concept of development in post-colonial Africa (meaning and indicators)
sla_name: Development in Post-Colonial Africa: Meaning and Indicators
sla_assessment_criteria: The concept of development in post- colonial Africa is well explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Online resources on the concept of development in post- colonial Africa
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Development is a process of improvement in people's economic, social and political well-being. In post-colonial Africa it means progress since independence.
sla_notes_details: Development includes economic growth, industrialisation, better incomes and services, and freedom and participation. Indicators are Gross Domestic Product and per capita income, life expectancy, literacy and school enrolment, infant mortality, access to water and electricity, poverty rates, employment, and the Human Development Index (HDI). Political indicators include democracy, stability and human rights. Environmental sustainability and gender equality are added. Post-colonial development strategies included planning, nationalisation, and later liberalisation.
sla_notes_illustrations: A country whose per capita income and literacy rise while infant mortality falls shows development according to these indicators.
sla_notes_daily_life: A village which gets a new school, clinic and clean water shows development in daily life.
sla_exercise: Name two indicators of development.::Per capita income and life expectancy.||What does HDI stand for?::Human Development Index.||Give one political indicator of development.::Democracy or respect for human rights.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the history of development in Africa
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the history of development in post-colonial Africa
learning_activity_name: Appraise political, economic, and social developments in different regions of Africa from the 1960 to present (Eastern, Western, Southern and Northern Africa)
sla_name: Political, Economic and Social Developments in Africa Since 1960
sla_assessment_criteria: Political, economic and social developments in different regions of Africa from the 1960s to present are well evaluated.
sla_teaching_aids: ICT devices with contents political|Economic|Social developments in different regions of Africa from the 1960 to present
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Africa's regions experienced different developments after 1960. Eastern, Western, Southern and Northern Africa each show distinct trends.
sla_notes_details: Politically, most countries gained independence by the 1960s, went through one-party and military rule and after 1990 moved to multiparty politics. Southern Africa completed liberation with Zimbabwe (1980), Namibia (1990) and South Africa (1994). Economically, early growth gave way to debt and structural adjustment in the 1980s, and later to growth based on minerals, oil, services and telecoms. North Africa developed oil and tourism and experienced the Arab Spring (2011). West Africa has ECOWAS, oil in Nigeria and cocoa in Ghana, and East Africa has EAC, tourism and agriculture. Socially there were gains in education and health, growth of cities and improved technology, but inequality and HIV/AIDS remain challenges.
sla_notes_illustrations: Tanzania expanded primary and secondary education, built health facilities and improved mobile communication while economic reforms boosted growth.
sla_notes_daily_life: Access to mobile money, schools and clinics shows some of these developments.
sla_exercise: Which Southern African country became free in 1994?::South Africa.||Name a regional community in West Africa.::ECOWAS.||What was a social improvement in Africa after independence?::Expansion of education and health services.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the history of development in Africa
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the history of development in post-colonial Africa
learning_activity_name: Discuss the internal and external factors hindering political, social, technological and economic development in Africa from the 1960s to the present
sla_name: Factors Hindering Development in Africa
sla_assessment_criteria: The internal and external factors hindering political, social, technological, and economic development in Africa from the 1960s to the present are well discussed.
sla_teaching_aids: Online resources on internal|External factors hindering political|Social|Technological|Economic development in Africa from the 1960s to the present
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Africa's development since 1960 has been hindered by both internal and external factors.
sla_notes_details: Internal factors include political instability and conflicts, corruption and poor governance, weak institutions, dependence on primary commodities, poor infrastructure, lack of skills and technology, disease, rapid population growth, ethnic divisions and environmental problems such as drought. External factors include colonial legacy, unfair terms of trade, debt and structural adjustment conditions, neo-colonialism, Cold War interference, arms trade, exploitation by multinational corporations and climate change. Solutions involve good governance, investment in people, regional integration, diversification, fair trade and technology.
sla_notes_illustrations: A country that depends on one export crop suffers when world prices fall, showing the mix of internal dependence and external market factors.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers who cannot access roads and markets experience the effects of poor infrastructure.
sla_exercise: Give one internal factor hindering development in Africa.::Corruption or political instability.||Give one external factor.::Debt or unfair terms of trade.||How can regional integration help?::It enlarges markets and encourages cooperation.

main_competence_name: Conduct a project in History
specific_competence_name: Conduct a project in History
learning_activity_name: Complete and submit for assessment the project initiated in Form Five
sla_name: Completing and Submitting the History Project
sla_assessment_criteria: A project in History is well written and submitted for assessment.
sla_teaching_aids: Online resources conducting project in History
sla_references: TET(2023), HISTORY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Form Six students complete the project begun in Form Five and present it for assessment. The written report is the final product.
sla_notes_details: They finalise the analysis of sources, cross-check evidence, write the report with a clear structure, acknowledge sources with references, and use maps, charts or photographs. They present and defend the findings during a project presentation week and submit the final report after corrections. Assessment considers research question, use of evidence, analysis, organisation and presentation, and originality.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student who studied the history of a local monument presents oral testimonies and old photographs, concludes on its significance and submits the final report.
sla_notes_daily_life: Writing and presenting a project prepares students for university research and for careers involving documentation.
sla_exercise: Name two parts of a history project report.::Introduction and conclusion (or findings, references).||Why must sources be acknowledged?::To give credit and show the evidence used.||What happens at the project presentation week?::Students present and defend their reports.
